items.readable_text:
Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn about the two-way relationship between a chord and a radius (or diameter) passing through the midpoint of the chord.

Content:
Before we start, we need to note an important fact about isosceles triangles. Consider the isosceles triangle below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/71f5155f56c880d47f01bf34359a28b6]

Content:
Let's draw the median [MATH: \overline{CM}] of this triangle that bisects the base.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3af4a5d19a4b434cdf4d66e105441f77]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: \triangle AMC\cong\triangle BMC] by the SSS criterion. So corresponding parts of congruent triangles give [MATH: \angle AMC = \angle BMC]. Since they are a linear pair, each must be a right angle.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/0cd03550561b4c253b1db766c4292e35]

Content:
This means that the median [MATH: \overline{CM}] is also the height of the triangle corresponding to the side [MATH: \overline{AB}.]

Content:
Conversely, we can also show that the altitude corresponding to the base bisects the base. Therefore, we have the following result:

Content:
> The median of a triangle is the same as its height precisely when the triangle is isosceles and the median is drawn from the apex to the base.

Content:
Next, we’ll see how this symmetry shows that the radius to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord.

sections.normalized_html: In the circle above, point [MATH: O] is the center, and diameter [MATH: \overline{MN}] bisects chord [MATH: \overline{PQ}] at point [MATH: R.] Find [MATH: PQ] if the radius of the circle is [MATH: 13 \: \text{cm}] and [MATH: OR=5 \: \text{cm}.]
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/41c8069bc70ac9a8dfa04bd3f37eae04]

In the circle above, point [MATH: O] is the center, and diameter [MATH: \overline{MN}] bisects chord [MATH: \overline{PQ}] at point [MATH: R.] Find [MATH: PQ] if the radius of the circle is [MATH: 13 \: \text{cm}] and [MATH: OR=5 \: \text{cm}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, let's draw the radii [MATH: \overline{OP}] and [MATH: \overline{OQ}.]

Since [MATH: OP = OQ,] we have that [MATH: \triangle OPQ] is isosceles. In this triangle, [MATH: \overline{OR}] is the median drawn to the base. Thus, [MATH: \overline{OR}] is also a height, and we get [MATH: \overline{OR} \perp \overline{PQ}.]

Now [MATH: \triangle ORQ] is right. So, using the Pythagorean theorem, we have the following equation: [MATH: OR^{2} + RQ^{2}|= OQ^{2}; (5)^{2} + RQ^{2}|= (13)^{2}; 25 + RQ^{2}|= 169; RQ^{2}|= 144; RQ|= 12]

Therefore, we have that [MATH: PQ|= 2RQ; = 2 ⋅ 12; = 24cm.]

Now, we obtain that [MATH: OT|= OR − TR; = 34 − 18; = 16.]

Finally, [MATH: \triangle OTS] is right. So, using the Pythagorean theorem, we have the following equation: [MATH: OT^{2} + TS^{2}|= OS^{2}; (16)^{2} + TS^{2}|= (34)^{2}; 256 + TS^{2}|= 1156; TS^{2}|= 900; TS|= sqrt(900); = 30]

Therefore, we have that [MATH: QS|= 2TS; = 2 ⋅ 30; = 60cm.]

Let's draw the median [MATH: \overline{CM}] of this triangle that bisects the base.

Graphic:

Content:
Notice that [MATH: \triangle AMC\cong\triangle BMC] by the SSS criterion. So corresponding parts of congruent triangles give [MATH: \angle AMC = \angle BMC]. Since they are a linear pair, each must be a right angle.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/0cd03550561b4c253b1db766c4292e35]

Content:
This means that the median [MATH: \overline{CM}] is also the height of the triangle corresponding to the side [MATH: \overline{AB}.]

Content:
Conversely, we can also show that the altitude corresponding to the base bisects the base. Therefore, we have the following result:

Content:
> The median of a triangle is the same as its height precisely when the triangle is isosceles and the median is drawn from the apex to the base.

Content:
Next, we’ll see how this symmetry shows that the radius to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord.

- In [MATH: \triangle HOJ,] the segment [MATH: \overline{OK}] is the median that bisects the base.
- Since [MATH: \triangle HOJ] is isosceles, it follows that [MATH: \overline{OK}] is also a height of the triangle, which means that [MATH: \overline{OK} \perp \overline{HJ}.]

So, we have the following result:

The converse is also true:

> If a radius (diameter) intersects a chord of a circle and is perpendicular to the chord, then the radius (diameter) bisects the chord.

Item 6 — Example: Finding the Length of a Chord When the Diameter Bisects the Chord

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/41c8069bc70ac9a8dfa04bd3f37eae04]

In the circle above, point [MATH: O] is the center, and diameter [MATH: \overline{MN}] bisects chord [MATH: \overline{PQ}] at point [MATH: R.] Find [MATH: PQ] if the radius of the circle is [MATH: 13 \: \text{cm}] and [MATH: OR=5 \: \text{cm}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, let's draw the radii [MATH: \overline{OP}] and [MATH: \overline{OQ}.]

[IMG: /graphics/59718ca2c62efe8b72d7b2aabc4c913d]

Since [MATH: OP = OQ,] we have that [MATH: \triangle OPQ] is isosceles. In this triangle, [MATH: \overline{OR}] is the median drawn to the base. Thus, [MATH: \overline{OR}] is also a height, and we get [MATH: \overline{OR} \perp \overline{PQ}.]

Now [MATH: \triangle ORQ] is right. So, using the Pythagorean theorem, we have the following equation:
[MATH: OR^{2} + RQ^{2}|= OQ^{2}; (5)^{2} + RQ^{2}|= (13)^{2}; 25 + RQ^{2}|= 169; RQ^{2}|= 144; RQ|= 12]

Therefore, we have that
[MATH: PQ|= 2RQ; = 2 ⋅ 12; = 24cm.]

In the circle above, point [MATH: O] is the center, and diameter [MATH: \overline{PR}] is perpendicular to chord [MATH: \overline{QS}] at point [MATH: T.] Find [MATH: QS] if the radius of the circle is [MATH: 34 \: \text{cm}] and [MATH: TR=18 \: \text{cm}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, let's draw the radii [MATH: \overline{OQ}] and [MATH: \overline{OS}.]

[IMG: /graphics/ed730e4c400a13b56aec04d2d6edc664]

Since [MATH: OQ = OS,] we have that [MATH: \triangle OSQ] is isosceles. In this triangle, [MATH: \overline{OT}] is the height drawn to the base. Thus, [MATH: \overline{OT}] is also a median, and we get [MATH: TS = TQ.]

Now, we obtain that
[MATH: OT|= OR − TR; = 34 − 18; = 16.]

Finally, [MATH: \triangle OTS] is right. So, using the Pythagorean theorem, we have the following equation:
[MATH: OT^{2} + TS^{2}|= OS^{2}; (16)^{2} + TS^{2}|= (34)^{2}; 256 + TS^{2}|= 1156; TS^{2}|= 900; TS|= sqrt(900); = 30]

Therefore, we have that
[MATH: QS|= 2TS; = 2 ⋅ 30; = 60cm.]
